properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Trajan's moneyers struck the gold aurei, silver denarii, and bronze sestertii that funded the Dacian and Parthian wars from the mint near the Capitoline. Every provincial city that struck its own coin copied the portrait these dies set. In 117 CE it was the single busiest mint in the Mediterranean world.
sources: NGC Ancients: Mints of the Roman Empire, ngccoin.com/news/article/8151
Ostia-Antica.org, 'The Maxentian Mint at Ostia' (Rome mint topography note)

properties.name: Lyon
properties.one_line: Augustus opened Lugdunum as the empire's second mint in 15 BCE, and for nearly a century it struck gold and silver alongside Rome. Its last major precious-metal issue ran under Vespasian in the 70s CE, and by Trajan's reign the workshop sat dormant, its output folded entirely into Rome. It stayed idle for another 180 years, until Diocletian revived it in 297 CE.
sources: NGC Ancients: Mints of the Roman Empire, ngccoin.com/news/article/8151
Aeternitas Numismatics, 'Knowing the Roman imperial mints: VIII - Lugdunum', aeternitas-numismatics.com
Cambridge, Journal of Roman Studies, 'The Mints of the Empire: Vespasian to Diocletian'

properties.name: Antioch
properties.one_line: Antioch struck silver tetradrachms bearing Trajan's portrait to pay the legions massing for his Parthian invasion, each coin stamped with an eagle gripping a club on the reverse. With Hadrian stationed here as governor of Syria, the city functioned as the empire's forward capital in 117 CE.
sources: McAlee, R., The Coinage of Antioch
Ancient Coin Traders, Trajan AR Tetradrachm, Antioch 98-99 CE, RPC/Prieur plate coin

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.one_line: Alexandria ran Egypt's closed currency system, striking billon tetradrachms that were illegal to carry across the province's border. Anyone arriving had to trade denarii for local coin at the frontier. Trajan's tetradrachm issue turned out to be the only major Egyptian silver coinage of the entire second century.
sources: Howgego, C., 'Coinage and the Roman Economy in the Antonine Period: the view from Egypt', Oxford Roman Economy Project, oxrep.classics.ox.ac.uk
Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2005.07.64, 'Coinage in Roman Egypt: The Hoard Evidence'

properties.name: Caesarea
properties.one_line: Caesarea, seat of Judaea's Roman governor, struck its own bronze coinage showing Tyche crowned with a city wall and altars to the emperor. A dated issue from around 115 CE proves the mint was still running just before the Kitos War tore through the province.
sources: RPC III 3954, Trajan, Caesarea Maritima AE

properties.name: Kayseri
properties.one_line: Caesarea in Cappadocia ran the largest provincial mint outside Alexandria, striking silver drachms and didrachms to pay the legions guarding the Armenian frontier. Its heaviest Trajanic issue, three light tetradrachm types struck in 112-114 CE during his sixth consulship, pictured Mount Argaeus and a kneeling camel of Arabia.
sources: Butcher, K. & Ponting, M., Numismatic Chronicle 175 (2015), silver coinage of Cappadocia, warwick.ac.uk offprint
Vcoins, Trajan AR Drachm, Caesarea Cappadocia, Arabia standing type

properties.name: Izmit
properties.one_line: Nicomedia, metropolis of Bithynia, was one of about fourteen city mints striking bronze coin across the province under Trajan. Each coin carried the emperor's portrait on one face and a local civic type on the other, part of a regional currency system that ran parallel to Rome's.
sources: Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2024.07.03, 'Between Roman culture and local tradition: Roman provincial coinage of Bithynia and Pontus during the reign of Trajan (98-117 AD)'
Academia.edu, 'The Roman Imperial Coinage Model for Some Provincial Coins of Bithynia and Pontus Struck During the Reign of Trajan (98-117)'

properties.name: Pergamon
properties.one_line: Pergamon's mint had struck the broad silver cistophorus since the 2nd century BCE, and Rome kept the coin alive as Asia's standard high-value currency, worth three denarii. Trajan's moneyers continued the type through his reign, carrying forward a design older than the province itself.
sources: American Numismatic Society, 'Attalid Cistophori and Roman Foreign Affairs in Asia Minor', numismatics.org/pocketchange/attalids
Academia.edu, 'The Introduction of Roman Coinages in Asia (133 BC-1st Century AD)'

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: Ephesus shared cistophorus production with Pergamon as one of only two workshops supplying Asia's silver currency, its busy harbor making it the easiest point to ship new coin around the province. Its own civic bronze ran alongside, stamped with the names of local magistrates each year.
sources: Forum Ancient Coins discussion board, 'The Coinage of Ephesus'
Coin World, 'Cistophori of Roman emperor Hadrian began with overstriking of older coins'

properties.name: Smyrna
properties.one_line: Smyrna ran a civic bronze mint under local magistrates and sophists, its dies carrying Zeus Akraios from his temple on Mount Pagus and the city's twin patron goddesses, the Nemeses. The mint's output continued without interruption through Trajan's nineteen-year reign.
sources: Art Institute of Chicago, 'Coin Depicting the God Zeus Akraios'
Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 'Coin of Smyrna with bust of Zeus Akraios'

properties.name: Sardis
properties.one_line: Sardis, where Lydian kings first struck coinage some seven centuries earlier, kept its own civic bronze mint running through the Roman principate. Its Roman-era coins paired the emperor's portrait with local Lydian imagery, a small echo of the city's ancient monetary fame.
sources: Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2019.06.19, 'Coins from the Excavations at Sardis'
Numista, 'The Bronze Coinage of Lydia, Sardes (Sardis), Tripolis'

properties.name: Tarsus
properties.one_line: Tarsus struck silver tetradrachms under Trajan pairing the emperor's bust with Tyche and the river-god Cydnus, the waterway running through the city's center. Cilicia's leading city was one of the few provincial mints trusted with silver rather than bronze alone.
sources: RPC II 754, Trajan, Tarsus AR Tetradrachm
Ancient Numismatic Mythology, 'Coinage of Cilicia', ancientcoinage.org

properties.name: Iznik
properties.one_line: Nicaea struck bronze coins under Trajan showing an altar on the reverse, one of roughly a dozen Bithynian cities licensed to mint their own small change. The city's rivalry with neighboring Nicomedia for the title of Bithynia's leading city played out partly through competing coin types.
sources: Academia.edu, 'Coins of the Bithynian Mint of Nicaea from the Viminacium Necropolis of Pecine'

properties.name: Apamea Cibotus
properties.one_line: Apamea, founded around 270 BCE by the Seleucid king Antiochus I and known to Romans as Cibotus, kept a civic bronze mint running into Trajan's reign under local high priests named on the coin legends. The city sat at a major road junction in Phrygia, feeding the wider trade that filled its treasury.
sources: Forum Ancient Coins, 'Ancient Greek Coins of Phrygia'

properties.name: Laodicea on the Lycus
properties.one_line: Laodicea, a wool and banking city so wealthy it rebuilt itself after a major earthquake without imperial aid, struck civic bronze honoring Trajan's wife Plotina as Augusta, a title she held from 105 CE. That dated issue fixes the mint's activity squarely within Trajan's reign.
sources: RPC III 2320, Plotina, Laodicea ad Lycum

properties.name: Tripoli
properties.one_line: Tripolis took its name from the three Phoenician cities, Tyre, Sidon, and Arados, that jointly founded it, and it kept a semi-autonomous civic mint striking small bronze coin for local trade. Its types carried Tyche and the twin caps of the Dioskuri, symbols the city had used since the Hellenistic era.

properties.name: Tyre
properties.one_line: Tyre's mint had gone silent for silver since Nero ended its famous shekel series in 65 CE, but Trajan revived it, striking tetradrachms again through his reign and into Hadrian's first year. The renewed coins carried an eagle gripping a club, no longer branded as an independent city issue but struck explicitly for the emperor.
sources: Coin World, 'The Shekels of Tyre: Ancients Today'

properties.name: Sidon
properties.one_line: Sidon struck civic bronze without a break for close to a century and a half, from Augustus through Hadrian, naming itself sacred and inviolate in its coin legends. Its types ranged from Tyche and Zeus to war galleys and Astarte riding in her sacred cart.

properties.name: Beirut
properties.one_line: Berytus, a Roman colony settled by veterans of two legions under Augustus and grown to roughly 50,000 people by Trajan's reign, struck its own bronze coinage showing a priest yoking oxen, the standard emblem of a newly founded colony. A dated issue survives from within Trajan's 98-117 reign.

properties.name: Ashkelon
properties.one_line: Ascalon opened Trajan's reign with a fresh bronze issue in its own civic year 129, equal to 98 CE, showing Nike striding with a palm branch and wreath. The free city counted its years from its own charter of freedom rather than Rome's calendar, advertising the autonomy its coinage represented.
sources: Forum Ancient Coins, 'Pseudo-Autonomous Roman Provincial Coins'

properties.name: Cyzicus
properties.one_line: Cyzicus struck its own bronze coinage under Trajan from a mint beside the isthmus linking the Kapidag peninsula to the Mysian mainland. Its dies paired the emperor's portrait with local gods like Kore Soteira across dozens of distinct Trajanic types. The city's harbor made it one of the busiest ports on the Sea of Marmara, feeding trade for the whole province of Asia.
sources: Aeternitas Numismatics, 'Knowing the Roman imperial mints: VII - Cyzicus'
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Cyzicus, Erdek, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Bursa
properties.one_line: Prusa ad Olympum, set on the northern slopes of Mount Olympus of Mysia, struck civic bronze coin under Trajan as one of fourteen minting cities across Bithynia and Pontus. Its coins carried the emperor's portrait on one face and local river gods on the other, following the same regional currency system as neighboring Nicaea and Nicomedia. The mint sat idle for long stretches before and after his reign, so its Trajanic issues survive as some of the rarest coins the city ever struck.
sources: RPC III 1035-1049, Trajan, Prusa ad Olympum
Harvard Art Museums, 'Coin of Prusa ad Olympum under Trajan'
properties.image_credit: Roman sculpture, Bursa Archaeological Museum · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Bosra
properties.one_line: Trajan's general Cornelius Palma folded the Nabataean kingdom into Rome in 106 CE, and the new provincial capital took the name Nova Trajana Bostra in his honor. Its mint struck silver tridrachms and drachms stamped with a camel, the animal that had carried the region's incense trade for centuries. Legio III Cyrenaica garrisoned the city, guarding the new Via Traiana Nova running south all the way to the Red Sea.
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre, Bosra, Syria · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Sepphoris
properties.one_line: Sepphoris, the largest city in Galilee, struck its first city-coinage under Trajan, stamping a palm tree flanked by two bunches of dates on the reverse of its bronze. The Greek legend on the obverse recorded that the emperor himself had granted the city this right. That grant did not last long: minting stopped before his reign ended, likely a penalty for the city's role in the 115-117 revolt, and coin did not flow from Sepphoris again until Antoninus Pius.
sources: Judaism and Rome, 'City-Coin of Sepphoris depicting the head of Trajan and a palm tree'
CoinWeek, David Hendin, 'Coins Tell the Story of Ancient Sepphoris'
properties.image_credit: Dionysus mosaic floor, Sepphoris, Israel · Wikimedia Commons (photo Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA)

properties.name: Hierapolis
properties.one_line: Hierapolis, famous even in antiquity for its blinding white travertine terraces, struck civic bronze under Trajan showing Athena standing beside Hermes with his money-bag and caduceus. The mint had been running since the 2nd century BCE, long before Rome arrived in Asia. A sacred hot spring fed the city's baths and gave the site its reputation as a place where gods and healing waters met.
sources: RPC I 2982 and RPC III (Trajan-period issues), Hierapolis, Phrygia
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Hierapolis, Pamukkale, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Perge
properties.one_line: Perge struck bronze under Trajan showing a temple front holding the cult statue of Artemis Pergaia with an eagle in the pediment, plus a smaller issue pairing his portrait with a harbor prow and lighthouse. The river Cestrus carried ships two miles inland to reach the city's gates. Perge's games and processions honoring Artemis drew visitors from across Pamphylia every year.
properties.image_credit: Overview of the ruins of Perge, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ankara
properties.one_line: Ancyra struck semi-autonomous bronze coin under Trajan, whose armies marched through the city in 113 CE on their way to the Parthian front, the first emperor known to have passed through it in person. The walls of its Temple of Augustus and Rome, built decades earlier, still carried the full engraved text of the Res Gestae, Augustus's own account of his reign, letting any literate visitor read the deified founder's memoir in stone. Galatia's capital sat at the crossroads where roads from the Bosphorus, the Black Sea, and Cappadocia all met.
sources: RPC III 3115, Ankyra, Galatia, semi-autonomous AE
properties.image_credit: Temple of Augustus and Rome, Ankara, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons (photo Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA)

properties.name: Samsun
properties.one_line: Amisus struck bronze under Trajan showing Nike striding with a palm branch and wreath, coinage issued long after the mint's earlier heyday under the Kings of Pontus. The free city had kept the right to strike its own coin as a reward for backing Rome during the Mithridatic Wars two centuries before. Its harbor made it the commercial capital of the entire province of Pontus.
sources: RPC I 2145, 2154; RPC II 729, Trajan, Amisus
properties.image_credit: Display case, Samsun Archaeology Museum, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Sinop
properties.one_line: Sinope, a Roman colony since Julius Caesar planted veterans there, struck bronze under Trajan alongside the dozen other city mints of Bithynia and Pontus. Its Roman-era bathhouse, later converted into the Balatlar church, still stands with walls thick enough to have survived two thousand years of Black Sea storms. Diogenes the Cynic, the philosopher who supposedly lived in a barrel, was born in this same harbor town almost five centuries earlier.
properties.image_credit: Balatlar Church, a Roman-era bath building, Sinop, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Cyrene
properties.one_line: Cyrene struck silver hemidrachms and bronze coin under Trajan pairing his portrait with the horned head of Zeus Ammon, the oracle god whose desert shrine had drawn pilgrims for seven centuries. An earthquake struck the region hard in 115 CE, badly damaging the city's Temple of Zeus even as its mint kept striking coin through the rest of the reign. Jewish rebels devastated much of Cyrenaica the following year in the Kitos War.
sources: RPC III 3, Trajan, Cyrene AR Hemidrachm
properties.image_credit: Temple of Zeus, Cyrene, Libya · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Paphos
properties.one_line: The Koinon of Cyprus, the island's confederation of cities, struck bronze coin under Trajan stamped with the conical black stone of the Temple of Aphrodite at Paphos, the goddess's most sacred shrine anywhere in the ancient world. Metal analysis shows these Trajanic issues were struck from dies cut in Rome and shipped out for use on the island. Paphos itself served as the political capital of Roman Cyprus, and its Houses of Dionysos and Theseus already carried some of the mosaic floors still visible today.
sources: Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 'Coin of Koinon of Cyprus with bust of Trajan'
Kyprios Character, 'Cypriote coinage under Roman rule (30 BC - 3rd century AD)'
properties.image_credit: Roman mosaics, Paphos Archaeological Park, Cyprus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Amasra
properties.one_line: Amastris took shape when four smaller Paphlagonian towns merged under a Persian-descended queen who gave the new city her name, and it was still striking its own bronze four centuries later under Trajan. Its Trajanic issues carried the war god Ares on one type and the personification Hope on another, part of a set of motifs it shared with neighboring Nicaea and Nicomedia. Twin harbors on a narrow peninsula made the town one of the safest anchorages on the whole Black Sea coast.
properties.image_credit: Amasra (ancient Amastris), Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Prusias ad Hypium
properties.one_line: Prusias ad Hypium, renamed from Cierus for the Bithynian king who once ruled it, struck civic bronze under Trajan showing the goddess Pax on its reverse. Its Roman theater, carved into the hillside above the Hypius river valley, is still largely intact and open to visitors today. The city stood along the inland road linking the Bithynian coast to the interior of Asia Minor.
sources: RPC III 1101-1103, Trajan, Prusias ad Hypium
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre, Prusias ad Hypium, Konuralp, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Karadeniz Eregli
properties.one_line: Heraclea Pontica struck bronze coin under Trajan, including a dated issue from 114-116 CE that helps anchor the chronology of the whole regional currency of Bithynia and Pontus. Colonists from Megara had founded the city on this Black Sea harbor nearly seven centuries earlier, and it once ruled a wide stretch of the southern coast as an independent Hellenistic kingdom before Rome absorbed it. Under Trajan its mint output made up close to a sixth of all known coin emissions from the province's fourteen minting cities.
sources: RPC III 1161-1177, esp. 1176, Trajan, Heraclea Pontica
Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2024.07.03, 'Roman provincial coinage of Bithynia and Pontus during the reign of Trajan'
properties.image_credit: Historical map of Heraclea Pontica · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Kadikoy
properties.one_line: Chalcedon struck bronze coin under Trajan as one of Bithynia's oldest cities, founded by Greek settlers from Megara more than seven centuries before his reign. Ancient writers mocked its founders as 'the blind' for choosing this shore when the far richer harbor of Byzantium sat empty just across the strait. Excavations beneath the modern Haydarpasa train station have since turned up ancient bath complexes buried under the city for two thousand years.
sources: The Archaeologist, 'Unearthing the Secrets of Ancient Chalcedon Beneath Modern Kadikoy'
properties.image_credit: 19th-century engraving of the Council of Chalcedon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Alasehir
properties.one_line: Philadelphia, founded by King Attalus II and named for his devotion to his brother, struck civic bronze under Trajan showing the goddess Cybele enthroned with a lion at her feet. Frequent earthquakes had shaken the city so often in earlier centuries that Rome once excused it from paying tribute. The Book of Revelation's letter to the seven churches of Asia names Philadelphia as the one church Christ found no fault in.
properties.image_credit: Ruins at Alasehir (ancient Philadelphia), Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Corinth
properties.one_line: Corinth struck civic bronze under Trajan a century and a half after Julius Caesar refounded the city as a Roman colony on ground the Greeks had abandoned since 146 BCE. Its coin types pictured the temples ringing the forum, among them the Archaic Temple of Apollo, whose seven surviving Doric columns had already stood for roughly six hundred years by Trajan's reign. The colony's harbors on two seas made it one of the wealthiest trading cities in the province of Achaia.
sources: Forum Ancient Coins NumisWiki, 'Corinth Coins and Cults'
properties.image_credit: Temple of Apollo, Corinth, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Nicopolis
properties.one_line: Nicopolis, the 'City of Victory' Augustus founded on the site of his own camp before the Battle of Actium, saw its civic mint flourish anew under Trajan, whose issues hailed him as savior of the city. Sometime between 103 and 114 CE Trajan split Epirus off from Achaia as its own imperial province, with Nicopolis as capital. Actium's naval battle, fought in the straits visible from the city walls, had decided who would rule the whole Roman world a century and a half earlier.
sources: RPC Online, type 8948, Trajan, Nicopolis, Epirus
Academia.edu, 'Actia Nicopolis. Coinage, Currency and Civic Identity (27BC - AD268)'
properties.image_credit: Roman aqueduct of Nicopolis, Preveza, Greece · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Anazarbus
properties.one_line: Anazarbus, calling itself Caesarea in its own official coin legends, struck bronze under Trajan dated to civic year 132, equal to 113-114 CE, pairing his portrait with that of his wife Plotina. The city would later become metropolis of Cilicia Secunda, but even under Trajan it already ranked as Cilicia's second city after Tarsus. A ring of hills studded with a much later Armenian fortress still frames the wide plain where the ancient ruins spread today.
sources: RPC III 3369, 3370, Trajan and Plotina, Anazarbus (as Caesarea Anazarbus)
CNG Coin Shop, 'CILICIA, Anazarbus (as Caesarea Anazarbus). Trajan, with Plotina'
properties.image_credit: General view of the ruins of Anazarbus, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Tios
properties.one_line: Tium struck bronze under Trajan as a small but independent mint among the fourteen minting cities of Bithynia and Pontus, its dies skipping the shared regional designs some neighboring towns adopted. Milesian colonists had founded the city at the mouth of the Billaeus river in the 7th century BCE, centuries before Rome existed. Its harbor shipped timber cut from the forests of the Bithynian interior across the Black Sea.
properties.image_credit: Tios (Tium) ancient city site, Filyos, Turkey · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Alexandria Troas
properties.one_line: Alexandria Troas struck its own colonial bronze coinage under a charter granted by Augustus, stamping coins COL AVG TROAS in Latin rather than Greek like its Aegean neighbors. Its dies pictured Apollo Smintheus and a grazing horse, images tied to the Troad's legendary past. The mint kept running through Trajan's reign, one of only a handful of Roman colonies in Asia Minor with the right to strike its own coin.

properties.name: Assos
properties.one_line: Assos struck civic bronze coin from a mint perched above its steep harbor on the Gulf of Edremit, the same acropolis where Aristotle once ran a school of philosophy. Its coinage under the empire carried Athena's helmeted head, matching the temple that still dominates the site's high point. Trajan's portrait appeared on the obverse of Assos issues struck during his reign.

properties.name: Adramyttium
properties.one_line: Adramyttium ran a civic bronze mint on the gulf that still carries its name, serving as the assize center where Roman governors heard legal cases for the surrounding district of Mysia. Its coins under Trajan paired the emperor's portrait with local river-god and Dionysiac types. Founded as an Athenian colony centuries earlier, the city kept striking coin through the second century CE.

properties.name: Cyme
properties.one_line: Cyme, the largest city of the Aeolian confederacy, struck bronze coin under Trajan showing its eponymous Amazon queen alongside a grazing horse, the same horse type the city had used on its coinage since the fourth century BCE. Strabo ranked Cyme first among the twelve Aeolian cities of the coast. The mint's Roman-period output kept that centuries-old horse emblem alive on Trajanic dies.

properties.name: Ilium
properties.one_line: Ilium struck bronze coin on the site the Romans revered as the ancestral home of Aeneas and, through him, of Rome itself. Its dies carried the helmeted head of Athena Ilias and a standing statue of the goddess copied from her shrine in the city. Roman emperors treated the mint as a point of dynastic pride, and Ilium's long series of Athena-type bronzes ran continuously through Trajan's reign into the third century CE.
sources: CNG, 'Troas, Ilion - Founded on the Site of Ancient Troy', cngcoins.com

properties.name: Parium
properties.one_line: Parium struck colonial bronze coin on the Hellespont after veteran soldiers were settled there under the Second Triumvirate, giving it the Latin title Colonia Gemina Iulia Pariana. Its dies showed Aesculapius the healer and Diana Lucifera rather than the Greek civic types used at nearby Cyzicus. Coinage struck for Nerva just before Trajan's accession shows the colony's mint was active going into his reign.

properties.name: Miletus
properties.one_line: Miletus struck civic bronze under Trajan from a city that had minted coin since the seventh century BCE, among the very first anywhere to do so. Its Roman-period dies carried Apollo Didymaios, patron of the great oracle temple six miles down the Sacred Way at Didyma. The mint's output under Trajan ran alongside a major Roman-funded rebuilding of that same sanctuary.

properties.name: Tralles
properties.one_line: Tralles struck civic bronze on the fertile terraces above the Maeander valley, one of the wealthiest cities of the conventus of Asia under Roman rule. Its coinage carried the cult of Zeus Larasios, worshipped at a nearby sanctuary the city guarded as its own. Trajanic-era issues from the mint paired that local god with the emperor's portrait on the obverse.

properties.name: Magnesia ad Sipylum
properties.one_line: Magnesia ad Sipylum struck civic bronze from beneath Mount Sipylus, the mountain Homer named as the resting place of the grieving Niobe. Roman rebuilding after a catastrophic earthquake under Tiberius in 17 CE, which leveled twelve cities of Asia in one night, had already reshaped the town by Trajan's reign. Its Trajanic coinage carried the emperor's portrait alongside the city's river-god and mountain personification.
sources: RPC III (Nerva-Hadrian), Magnesia ad Sipylum, Lydia

properties.name: Magnesia on the Maeander
properties.one_line: Magnesia on the Maeander struck civic bronze centered on Artemis Leukophryene, whose temple in the city was ranked by ancient writers among the largest in Asia Minor, bigger by measurement than the Parthenon. Its Roman-period coin dies pictured the goddess in her distinctive local cult image. The mint kept producing bronze coin under Trajan alongside the continued upkeep of that temple.
sources: RPC III (Nerva-Hadrian), Magnesia ad Maeandrum, Ionia

properties.name: Halicarnassus
properties.one_line: Halicarnassus struck civic bronze from the harbor city that four and a half centuries earlier had built the Mausoleum, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, for its ruler Mausolus. Its Roman-era coin types carried Ares and Aphrodite, deities tied to the city's Carian and Greek double heritage. Trajan's portrait appeared on Halicarnassian bronze struck while the Mausoleum still stood largely intact above the harbor.

properties.name: Cnidus
properties.one_line: Cnidus struck civic bronze at the tip of a long Carian peninsula, home to the Aphrodite of Cnidus, the first fully nude female statue in Greek sculpture and one of Praxiteles' most famous works. Roman-period coin dies from the city carried Aphrodite's image, drawing tourists and pilgrims to see the original in her round temple. The mint remained active into Trajan's reign, striking coin for a city whose main export by then was its own statue's fame.

properties.name: Nysa
properties.one_line: Nysa struck civic bronze coin tied to the nearby sanctuary of Pluto and Kore at Acharaca, where ancient visitors believed a cave led directly into the underworld. Strabo himself described the site's healing rituals in detail. Trajan's portrait appeared on Nysa's bronze issues alongside types honoring that underworld cult, one of the more unusual civic identities struck on any Roman provincial coin.

properties.name: Thyatira
properties.one_line: Thyatira struck civic bronze in a Lydian textile and dyeing town later named among the seven churches addressed in the Book of Revelation. Its coin dies carried Apollo Tyrimnaios, the local sun-god, mounted on horseback, and referenced the city's active guilds of dyers, bronze-smiths, and wool-workers. Trajan's portrait ran on the obverse of Thyatiran bronze struck while the city's textile trade was at its Roman-period height.

properties.name: Mytilene
properties.one_line: Mytilene struck civic bronze as the chief city of Lesbos, a status it had held since Sappho and Alcaeus composed poetry there seven centuries before Trajan. The city held the rare privileged rank of civitas libera, a free ally of Rome exempt from direct provincial taxation. Its Roman-period coinage carried a lyre alongside the emperor's portrait, a nod to the island's literary fame.

properties.name: Cos
properties.one_line: Cos struck civic bronze on an island whose sanctuary of Asclepius drew the sick from across the Mediterranean, and whose most famous native son, Hippocrates, had founded a school of medicine there five centuries earlier. Roman-period coin dies from the mint carried Asclepius and his serpent staff. Trajan's portrait appeared on Coan bronze struck while the Asclepieion still functioned as one of the busiest healing centers of the ancient world.

properties.name: Rhodes
properties.one_line: Rhodes struck its own civic bronze under Rome, carrying on a coinage tradition that had run since the fifth century BCE and once financed the Colossus, the bronze statue that stood at the harbor mouth until an earthquake toppled it around 226 BCE. Its Roman-period dies kept the radiate head of Helios and the island's signature rose emblem. Rhodes held free-city status under Trajan, striking coin as an ally of Rome rather than a taxed provincial subject.

properties.name: Sagalassos
properties.one_line: Sagalassos struck civic bronze from a mountain city set more than 1,500 meters up in the Taurus range of Pisidia, one of the highest urban sites anywhere in the Roman world. Excavations at the site have recovered large quantities of its Roman-period small change, evidence of a busy local economy running on the city's own coin. Trajan's portrait ran on Sagalassian bronze struck during the same decades the city built its monumental fountain house, the Antonine Nymphaeum's predecessor.

properties.name: Termessos
properties.one_line: Termessos struck civic bronze from a fortress city wedged into a mountain gorge of Pisidia, a site so defensible that Alexander the Great chose not to attack it in 333 BCE. The Roman Senate had granted the city free and autonomous status in 71 BCE, and its coin dies kept advertising that title, ELEUTHERA AUTONOMOS, on Roman-period issues struck long afterward. Trajan's reign fell within that long stretch of self-governing coinage.
sources: CoinWeek, 'Ancient Coin Profiles: The Independent Bronze Coinage of Roman Termessos'

properties.name: Side
properties.one_line: Side struck civic bronze from Pamphylia's largest port, its very name meaning pomegranate in the pre-Greek Anatolian language the city's founders once spoke. Its coin dies carried that same pomegranate as a civic badge, stamped on issues for centuries before and after Trajan. The mint's Roman-period output supported a port city that doubled as a major regional slave market under the empire.

properties.name: Attaleia
properties.one_line: Attaleia struck civic bronze as capital of the province of Lycia et Pamphylia, founded three centuries earlier by King Attalus II of Pergamon as a naval base for his fleet. Its Roman-period coin types carried Poseidon holding a dolphin, a nod to the harbor that had made the city's fortune. The mint's Trajanic bronze paired that maritime god with the emperor's portrait on the obverse.

properties.name: Byzantium
properties.one_line: Byzantium struck civic bronze from the peninsula between the Bosporus and the Golden Horn, a defensive position so strong it survived sieges for a thousand years before Constantine ever chose it as his new capital. Its coin dies carried a bull standing on a dolphin, recalling the legendary cow that guided the city's Megarian founders across the strait. Byzantium was counted among the handful of Bithynian-region cities striking coin without an imperial portrait during Trajan's reign, a mark of its old semi-autonomous standing.
sources: Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2024.07.03, 'Between Roman culture and local tradition: Roman provincial coinage of Bithynia and Pontus during the reign of Trajan (98-117 AD)'

properties.name: Gadara
properties.one_line: Gadara struck civic bronze as one of the ten Greek cities of the Decapolis, perched on a ridge overlooking the Sea of Galilee and the Yarmuk River gorge. Its coins were dated by a local era counted from 64 BCE, when Pompey freed the city from Hasmonaean rule, so a Trajanic-era coin from Gadara carries a year number well past 160 in its own local reckoning. The city was known in antiquity as a center of Greek learning, home to the poet Meleager and the satirist Menippus.

properties.name: Gaza
properties.one_line: Gaza struck civic bronze dated by its own local era counted from 61 BCE, when Aulus Gabinius rebuilt the city after Alexander Jannaeus had razed it decades before. Its coin dies carried Marnas, the city's chief god, worshipped at the Marneion temple that ranked among the largest religious sanctuaries in the region. Gaza's Trajanic-era bronze kept that local calendar running rather than counting years from the emperor's own reign.
sources: Israel Numismatic Society, Farhi, Y., 'The City of Gaza in the Roman Period'
Academia.edu, Farhi, Y. (2015), 'Cleopatra in Gaza(?): A Hitherto Unpublished Coin Type from Gaza and the First Year of Coinage in Gaza under Roman Rule', American Journal of Numismatics 27

properties.name: Neapolis
properties.one_line: Neapolis struck civic bronze from a city Vespasian founded fresh in 72 CE at the foot of Mount Gerizim, the mountain the Samaritans held sacred as their true temple site. Its coin dies carried a detailed rendering of that mountain's summit, staircase, and temple, a landscape portrait almost unique among Roman provincial coin types. The mint's bronze under Trajan continued a local coinage tradition begun barely two decades earlier under Domitian.
sources: Journal of Roman Archaeology, 'A Roman altar on Mount Gerizim: Rediscovering a civic icon on tetradrachms of Neapolis (Samaria)'
Near Eastern Archaeology 74.3, 'From Mountain to Icon: Mount Gerizim on Roman Provincial Coins from Neapolis, Samaria'

properties.name: Laodicea ad Mare
properties.one_line: Laodicea ad Mare struck civic bronze from a Syrian port city Seleucus I founded and named for his mother, ranked among the four sister cities of the Syrian Tetrapolis alongside Antioch. A dated bronze diassarion from the mint places an issue precisely in 114/115 CE, within Trajan's Parthian campaign years, when Laodicea served as a supply port for the eastern war effort. The city's dies carried Tyche wearing her turreted crown, the standard emblem of Roman Syria's civic mints.
sources: RPC III (Nerva-Hadrian), Laodicea ad Mare, Syria
Coins Legacy, 'Syria, Seleucis and Pieria, Laodicea ad Mare Mint, Trajan, AE Diassarion, CY 162 = 114/5 AD'

properties.name: Athens
properties.one_line: Athens struck civic bronze under its own magistrates rather than an imperial governor, a privilege tied to the free-city status Rome had granted the city for its classical legacy. Its Roman-period dies kept the owl and olive spray of Athena, the same emblems that had marked Athenian silver coinage six centuries earlier. Excavations of the Athenian Agora have recovered these civic bronzes from Trajan's reign alongside everyday market debris, proof the coin actually circulated where it was struck.
sources: Kroll, J. H., The Athenian Agora XXVI: The Greek Coins (Princeton, 1993)

properties.name: Patrae
properties.one_line: Patrae struck colonial bronze coin after Augustus resettled the city with veterans of Actium and renamed it Colonia Augusta Aroe Patrensis, folding in the populations of several smaller neighboring towns. Its Latin-legend coin dies pictured a priest plowing the ritual furrow that marked a Roman colony's founding boundary. The mint's output under Trajan served a city that had grown, under Roman patronage, into the busiest port of western Achaia.

properties.name: Thessalonica
properties.one_line: Thessalonica struck civic bronze as the seat of Macedonia's Roman governor and the meeting place of the province's koinon, its coin dies carrying the Cabiri, twin gods worshipped locally as protectors of sailors on the Thermaic Gulf. Founded by Cassander in 315 BCE and named for a half-sister of Alexander the Great, the city sat astride the Via Egnatia, the main overland route linking Rome to its eastern provinces. Trajan's portrait ran on Thessalonican bronze struck while that highway carried the empire's traffic east toward the Parthian front.

properties.name: Philippi
properties.one_line: Philippi struck colonial bronze coin after Octavian and Antony resettled the battlefield where they had defeated Caesar's assassins in 42 BCE, planting veteran colonists on the plain below the city's acropolis. Its Latin-legend dies carried three military standards, a direct reference to the legions once stationed there, and the colony's official title, Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensis. The mint kept striking that same colonial imagery through Trajan's reign, a century and a half after the battle that founded it.

properties.name: Kemerhisar
properties.one_line: Tyana struck a Trajan silver tridrachm stamped with a bundle of grain ears, celebrating the wheatfields of its Cappadocian plain, alongside bronze issues pairing Zeus enthroned with a bull. The city stood at the foot of the Taurus Mountains beside the road linking the Cilician Gates to the interior, a chokepoint every army marching east had to pass through. Its mint ran independently of nearby Caesarea, giving Cappadocia two active civic coinages under Trajan.
sources: Forum Ancient Coins, Members' Coin Gallery, 'Trajan - Tyana Cappadocia'

properties.name: Yumurtalik
properties.one_line: Aegeae, a small port on the Bay of Issus, struck silver tetradrachms and bronze coin without a break from 20 BCE onward, including an issue dated to the very transition between Trajan and Hadrian in 117-118 CE. Its dies paired the emperor's portrait with Perseus and the curved harpa he used to behead Medusa. Strabo already described the city as a modest harbor town by the time Rome absorbed Cilicia.
sources: Academia.edu, 'Additions and Corrections to the Numismatic Corpus of Aegeae (Cilicia)'

properties.name: Yakapinar
properties.one_line: Mopsuestia struck bronze civic coin on the Pyramus River continuously from Domitian through Caracalla, with silver appearing only in rare exceptional issues. The city claimed the seer Mopsus, son of Apollo, as its legendary founder and namesake. A stone bridge across the Pyramus, rebuilt in the Roman era, still stands at the site today.
sources: Ancient Numismatic Mythology, 'Coinage of Cilicia', ancientcoinage.org

properties.name: Kiziltahta
properties.one_line: Mallus struck civic bronze under Trajan naming itself devoted to the oracle-hero Amphilochus, whose local shrine supposedly answered questions for a fee of two obols. The city sat where the Pyramus River met the sea, facing its own satellite port of Magarsus across the water. Its coin legends ran continuously from Tiberius through Macrinus, spanning more than a century of civic minting.
sources: Ancient Numismatic Mythology, 'Coinage of Cilicia', ancientcoinage.org

properties.name: Amasya
properties.one_line: Amaseia struck bronze coin under Trajan showing a five-stepped temple and a legend dated to local year 115, corresponding to 112-113 CE. Strabo, the geographer who wrote the fullest surviving account of the ancient world, was born in this city carved into a gorge of the Iris River. Rock-cut tombs of the old Pontic kings still loom over the site from cliffs above the riverbank.
sources: Bryn Mawr Classical Review 2024.07.03, 'Roman provincial coinage of Bithynia and Pontus during the reign of Trajan'

properties.name: Kutahya
properties.one_line: Cotiaeum struck civic bronze under Trajan honoring Zeus Melenos, a local title of the god tied to a mountain shrine outside the city. The Roman proconsul Marcus Scapula, who governed Asia during Trajan's reign, appears named as issuing magistrate on the city's dies. Set on the upper Tembris River, Cotiaeum sat along the road linking Dorylaeum to the road hub at Apamea sixty miles south.
sources: Numis Forums, 'Off the Beaten Path: Cotiaeum (Phrygia) Zeus'

properties.name: Tel Dor
properties.one_line: Dora struck a burst of bronze coin in a single year, 111-112 CE, pairing Trajan's portrait with a turreted Tyche and a river god swimming at her feet. Only eleven examples of that issue are known today, making it one of the rarest civic coinages on the whole Phoenician coast. The old Canaanite port, first settled more than a thousand years before Rome existed, used the coinage to mark a moment of renewed civic standing under Trajan.

properties.name: Eskihisar
properties.one_line: Stratonicea struck bronze coin under Trajan showing Zeus seated on a throne with a patera in hand, a design its Seleucid founders would have recognized on coins struck three centuries earlier. The city took its name from Stratonice, wife of the Seleucid king Antiochus I, and grew wealthy from marble quarries still visible around the site. Its territory held two famous sanctuaries, including one to Zeus Panamaros reachable by a sacred processional road.
sources: RPC Online III 1772, Trajan, Stratonicea, Caria

properties.name: Marmara Ereglisi
properties.one_line: Perinthus struck civic bronze under Trajan showing Dionysus pouring wine at a flaming altar, part of a coinage program the city ran as capital of the Roman province of Thrace. Its dies also carried a long-running series on the labors of Heracles, from the Nemean lion to the golden apples. The city's harbor on the Sea of Marmara made it the administrative hub for a province stretching from the Aegean to the Danube foothills.
sources: RPC Online III 700, Trajan, Perinthus, Thrace

properties.name: Gortyna
properties.one_line: Gortyna struck imperial bronze coin without interruption from Augustus through Trajan's reign, the longest-running civic mint on Crete. The city's law code, carved into massive stone blocks in the 5th century BCE, still stands legible today as the oldest and most complete Greek law code ever recovered. Rome made Gortyna its provincial capital for Crete and Cyrenaica after Pompey's conquest of the island.
sources: Wikimedia Commons, Category: Ancient Roman bronze coins of Gortyna

properties.name: Sparti
properties.metal: none (dormant, revived under Hadrian in the 120s CE)
properties.one_line: Sparta's mint sat silent through all of Trajan's reign, its last civic bronze struck under Claudius roughly sixty years earlier. The city famous for its warrior culture would not strike coin again until the 120s CE, after Hadrian visited Achaia in person. In 117 CE Sparta was a market town living off its Classical-era reputation, its coin workshops idle for two generations running.
sources: Coin World, 'Sparta and its coinage: Ancients Today'
Sulla Coins, 'Where are all the Spartan coins?'

properties.name: Debelt
properties.one_line: Deultum, a colony Vespasian planted for veterans of the Eighth Legion, struck its own bronze coin under Trajan as Colonia Flavia Pacis Deultensium. It was one of only two Roman colonies with minting rights anywhere in the province of Thrace. Its coin legends ran in Latin rather than the Greek used at every civic mint around it, marking the settlement out as a transplanted island of Roman citizens on the Thracian coast.

properties.name: Pomorie
properties.one_line: Anchialus received formal city status from Trajan, who folded his own family name into it, and its coins carried the legend 'of the Ulpian Anchialitans' ever after in his honor. Salt pans along its shallow bay had drawn settlers to the site since the 5th century BCE. Within a century of that Trajanic charter, its Black Sea harbor became the busiest trading point in the whole province of Thrace.
sources: TrustedAncientCoins.com, 'Architecture on Ancient Greek and Roman Coins Guide'

properties.name: Chios
properties.one_line: Chios struck bronze coin under Trajan and Hadrian carrying the sphinx the island had used as its emblem for nearly nine centuries, one forepaw resting on an amphora or a ship's prow. The island had converted its old Greek denominations to the Roman assarion system a century earlier under Augustus, blending local tradition with imperial bookkeeping. Chian wine, prized across the Mediterranean, funded the civic treasury that kept the mint running.
sources: Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 'Coin of Chios with sphinx'

properties.name: Gazipasa
properties.metal: none (bronze coinage began only after 117 CE, as Traianopolis)
properties.one_line: Trajan died in this small Cilician port in August 117 CE, the first Roman emperor to die outside Italy. Selinus had no mint of its own at the time; the grieving city renamed itself Traianopolis and only began striking bronze coin picturing his temple afterward, output that continued into the 3rd century CE. A single historic moment turned a minor harbor town into a permanent fixture of imperial memory.
sources: FollowingHadrian.com, '8 August AD 117 - Trajan dies at Selinus'

properties.name: Acre
properties.one_line: Ptolemais, a Roman colony Claudius upgraded from an old Phoenician port town, struck bronze coin under Trajan pairing his portrait with a turreted Tyche seated on rocks and a river god at her feet. Its full colonial title ran Colonia Claudia Felix Ptolemais Germanica Stabilis, one of the longest city names in the Roman East. Ptolemy II had refounded the older Phoenician city under his own name four centuries earlier, and Rome layered a Latin identity on top of that Hellenistic one.
sources: Zuzim Coins, 'Akko - Ptolemais, Trajan AE, About Extremely Fine, 98-117 C.E.'
Academia.edu, 'The Mint of Akko through the Ages'

properties.name: Ballihisar
properties.one_line: Pessinus, seat of the Mother Goddess Cybele's most sacred shrine in Asia Minor, struck civic bronze through Trajan's reign under the oversight of Galatia's Roman governor. Its coin types kept returning to Cybele's image, the same goddess whose black meteorite stone Rome had imported to the capital three centuries earlier during the war with Hannibal. Scholars still debate whether Pessinus or neighboring Ancyra was the actual mint site behind some of the province's shared coin issues.
sources: Academia.edu, 'The Coinage of Pessinous: Iconography, Civic Identity and Roman Power'
